facts.statement: The genus Sinosauropteryx was described by Ji and Ji in 1996.
facts.quote: authority: Ji & Ji, 1996

facts.statement: The species was originally named Compsognathus prima before being reclassified as Sinosauropteryx prima.
facts.quote: synonyms: *Compsognathus prima (Ji & Ji, 1996)

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx was the first non-avian dinosaur taxon discovered with evidence of feathers.
facts.quote: Described in 1996, it was the first dinosaur taxon outside of Avialae (birds and their immediate relatives) to be found with evidence of feathers.

facts.statement: The dinosaur was covered in a coat of simple, filament-like feathers.
facts.quote: It was covered with a coat of very simple filament-like feathers.

facts.statement: Preserved feather structures indicate that Sinosauropteryx had a countershading body pattern and a banded tail.
facts.quote: Structures that indicate the colour pattern have also been preserved in some of its feathers, which show that Sinosauropteryx had a countershading pattern in its body with a banded tail.

facts.statement: The largest known specimen of Sinosauropteryx reached a length of 1.07 meters and an estimated weight of 0.55 kilograms.
facts.quote: The longest known specimen reaches up to 1.07 m in length, with an estimated weight of 0.55 kg.

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx was a small theropod characterized by an unusually long tail and short arms.
facts.quote: Sinosauropteryx was a small theropod with an unusually long tail and short arms.

facts.statement: While initially placed in the family Compsognathidae, later analyses placed Sinosauropteryx in its own family, Sinosauropterygidae.
facts.quote: It was considered a close relative of the similar but older genus Compsognathus, with both genera belonging to the family Compsognathidae, though subsequent analyses did not recover this family to be monophyletic and placed Sinosauropteryx within its own family, Sinosauropterygidae.

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx lived in northeastern China during the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Sinosauropteryx lived in what is now northeastern China during the early Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The first fossil specimen of Sinosauropteryx prima was uncovered in August 1996 by the fossil hunter Li Yumin.
facts.quote: The first fossil specimen of the dinosaur later named Sinosauropteryx prima was uncovered in August 1996 by Li Yumin.

facts.statement: All known fossils of Sinosauropteryx were found in the Yixian Formation in the Beipiao and Lingyuan regions of Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: All of the fossils were found in the Jianshangou or Dawangzhangzi Beds of the Yixian Formation in the Beipiao and Lingyuan regions of Liaoning, China.

facts.statement: The fossil beds containing Sinosauropteryx are dated to between 124.6 and 122 million years ago.
facts.quote: These fossil beds have been dated to 124.6–122 million years ago, during the early Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: A second species, Sinosauropteryx lingyuanensis, was named and described by Rui Qiu and colleagues in 2025.
facts.quote: In 2025, Rui Qiu and colleagues named and described a second species of Sinosauropteryx: S. lingyuanensis.

facts.statement: The holotype of S. lingyuanensis is a near-complete skeleton of a potential juvenile that preserves traces of feather integument.
facts.quote: The assigned holotype is IVPP V 12415, which comprises a near complete skeleton of a potential juvenile which also preserves traces of feather integument.

facts.statement: There is a debated alternative interpretation suggesting the filamentous impressions are collagen fibers rather than feathers, though this is not widely accepted.
facts.quote: Some contention has arisen with an alternative interpretation of the filamentous impression as remains of collagen fibres, but this has not been widely accepted.

facts.statement: Well-preserved fossils of Sinosauropteryx provide evidence regarding its diet and reproduction.
facts.quote: Well-preserved fossils of this genus illustrate many aspects of its biology, such as its diet and reproduction.

facts.statement: Researchers initially debated whether the filamentous structures on Sinosauropteryx were modern feathers or something else, with some suggesting they were stiffening structures from a frill.
facts.quote: the team agreed that the structures preserved on Sinosauropteryx were not modern feathers, but suggested further research was required to discover their exact nature

facts.statement: Some researchers proposed that the filaments were collagen fibers forming a frill on the back and underside of the tail, similar to modern aquatic lizards.
facts.quote: researchers interpreted the filamentous impressions around Sinosauropteryx fossils as remains of collagen fibres rather than primitive feathers

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx was a small bipedal theropod characterized by short arms, large first fingers, and a long tail.
facts.quote: Sinosauropteryx was a small bipedal theropod, noted for its short arms, large first finger (thumbs), and long tail

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Sinosauropteryx measured 68 cm in length, including the tail, making it one of the smallest known adult non-avian theropods.
facts.quote: The taxon includes some of the smallest known adult non-avian theropod specimens, with the holotype specimen measuring only 68 cm in length, including the tail

facts.statement: A later study estimated the mass of Sinosauropteryx to be 0.99 kg.
facts.quote: A subsequent paper estimated its mass to be 0.99 kg

facts.statement: The arms of Sinosauropteryx were only 30% the length of its legs, compared to 40% in Compsognathus.
facts.quote: The arms of Sinosauropteryx (humerus and radius) were only 30% the length of its legs (thigh bone and shin), compared to 40% in Compsognathus

facts.statement: The hands of Sinosauropteryx were about 84% to 91% the length of the rest of the arm and half the length of the foot.
facts.quote: Its hands were long compared to its arms, about 84% to 91% of the length of the rest of the arm (humerus and radius), and half the length of the foot

facts.statement: The teeth of Sinosauropteryx were heterodont, with slender, unserrated teeth near the tips of the upper jaws and serrated, laterally compressed teeth behind them.
facts.quote: The teeth differed slightly (they were heterodont) based on position: those near the tips of the upper jaws (on the premaxillae) were slender and lacked serrations, while those behind them (on the maxillae) were serrated and laterally compressed

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx had over 50 extremely elongated caudal vertebrae, constituting 60% of its body length.
facts.quote: that there are over 50 extremely elongated caudals, constituting 60% of the body length

facts.statement: The hind limb of Sinosauropteryx was long and robust, with the tibia only slightly longer than the femur.
facts.quote: the hind limb was long and robust, the tibia is only slightly longer than the femur

facts.statement: The tarsals of Sinosauropteryx were separated, and the metatarsals were relatively robust with unfused proximal ends.
facts.quote: the tarsals are separated, and the metatarsals are relatively robust with unfused proximal ends

facts.statement: Most paleontologists interpret the preserved filaments on Sinosauropteryx as a primitive type of feather.
facts.quote: All described specimens of Sinosauropteryx preserve integumentary structures (filaments arising from the skin) which most palaeontologists interpret as a primitive type of feathers.

facts.statement: The filaments increase in length along the body to reach 35 mm over the shoulder blades.
facts.quote: Going further along the body, the filaments rapidly increase in length until reaching lengths of 35 mm over the shoulder blades.

facts.statement: The filaments reach their maximum length of 40 mm midway down the tail.
facts.quote: The filaments lengthen again and reach their maximum length midway down the tail at 40 mm.

facts.statement: The longest feathers on the forearm measured 14 mm.
facts.quote: The longest feathers present on the forearm measured 14 mm.

facts.statement: Microscopic examination suggests the filaments were hollow, appearing dark at the edges and light internally, similar to modern feathers.
facts.quote: Microscopic examination shows that individual filaments appear dark along the edges and light internally, suggesting that they were hollow, like modern feathers.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that thick filaments being bundles of thin filaments is a more plausible hypothesis than them being a variant of quilled plumaceous feathers with a morphology opposite to birds.
facts.quote: Thus, the idea that thick filaments are simply bundles of thin filaments is less unusual than the idea that they were a variant of quilled plumaceous feathers which developed a morphology opposite that of birds and other feathered theropods.

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx had feather-like structures but was not very closely related to Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: While Sinosauropteryx had feather-like structures, it was not very closely related to the previous "first bird" Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: In a 2002 presentation, Longrich suggested that the banding patterns on Sinosauropteryx specimens preserve remnants of the animal's actual colouration.
facts.quote: Longrich suggested in his 2002 presentation for the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology that these specimens actually preserve remnants of the colouration pattern the animal would have exhibited in life.

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx is classified within the family Compsognathidae, a group of small, long-tailed coelurosaurian theropods.
facts.quote: Sinosauropteryx is generally classified in the family Compsognathidae, a group of small-bodied long-tailed coelurosaurian theropods known from the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous of Asia, Europe, and South America.

facts.statement: A 2024 study by Andrea Cau questioned the classification of Sinosauropteryx and related taxa, recovering them in a polytomy within basal Coelurosauria that excluded the genus Compsognathus.
facts.quote: In 2024, Andrea Cau published a study on the phylogenetics of compsognathids that called the assessment of these taxa into question.

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx lived approximately 120 million years ago during the Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Asia.

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx inhabited China during the Early Cretaceous and was likely a close relative of the genus Compsognathus.

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx was covered in simple feathers, though some researchers have debated whether these filamentous impressions represent collagen fibers instead of feathers.
facts.quote: El fósil, extremadamente bien preservado, muestra que Sinosauropteryx estuvo cubierto con una capa de plumas muy simples, aunque una cierta controversia presentó una interpretación alternativa de la impresión filamentosa como fibras del colágenos, pero esto no ha sido ampliamente aceptado.

facts.statement: The filaments of Sinosauropteryx had a simple two-branched structure similar to the primitive secondary feathers of the modern kiwi.
facts.quote: Estos filamentos consistían en una estructura ramificada en dos simple, muy similar a las plumas secundarias primitivas del moderno kiwi.

facts.statement: Sinosauropteryx is the first non-avian dinosaur in which coloration has been determined, showing a reddish tail with light bands.
facts.quote: En algunas de sus plumas también se han conservado estructuras que indican coloración, lo que hace Sinosauropteryx los primeros dinosaurios no aviares donde se ha determinado la coloración.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence from specimen NIGP 127587 shows that Sinosauropteryx ate small, fast-moving lizards like Dalinghosaurus.

facts.statement: Specimen NIGP 127587 contained several small eggs in its abdomen, providing evidence of reproduction in Sinosauropteryx.
facts.quote: The same specimen of S. prima which had preserved a lizard in its stomach contents (NIGP 127587) also had several small eggs in its abdomen.

facts.statement: The eggs of Sinosauropteryx measured 36 mm in length and 26 mm in width.

facts.statement: The climate of Sinosauropteryx's habitat was temperate with distinct seasons, averaging about 10°C annually, which implies unusually cold winters for the Mesozoic era likely due to high latitude.
facts.quote: The climate has been interpreted as temperate, with distinct wet and dry seasons. The yearly temperature during this time period averaged about 10 C, indicating a temperate climate with unusually cold winters for the generally warm Mesozoic era, possibly due to northern China's high latitude during this time.

facts.statement: The environment where Sinosauropteryx lived experienced periodic mortality events caused by volcanic eruptions, wildfires, and noxious gases.
